subject: zoology
question_text: 'Prevention is better than cure'. Justify with regard to TDA abuse.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.43, SAQ 45). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: What TDA means
lines: TDA means tobacco, drugs and alcohol.
Once a person becomes addicted to any of these,
the cure is long, costly and often incomplete.
Stopping the habit before it starts is therefore
easier than curing it, so the saying 'prevention
is better than cure' holds true for TDA abuse.
steps.why: The saying only becomes an argument once the difficulty of the cure is stated, so the opening step must say why curing an addiction is hard.
common_mistakes: Writing only the full form of TDA. The reason prevention is better is part of this mark.
Listing the measures here. They belong in the steps that follow.
steps.memory_tip: TDA is tobacco, drugs and alcohol. Cure is slow and uncertain, so prevention wins.
steps.margin_note: Full form first, then two lines of justification.

steps.label: Home and school
lines: Avoid undue parental pressure. Every child has
its own choices and capacity, and parents should
not force a child to perform beyond it or
compare the child with others in studies and
games.
Parents and teachers have a responsibility to
advise and counsel a child who is likely to fall
into TDA abuse.
steps.why: Most first use begins at home or at school, so the first measures name the two adults closest to the child and what each one should change.
common_mistakes: Writing 'parents should take care' with no measure named. Name the pressure and the counselling.
Writing that the child should be punished. Counselling, not punishment, is the measure.
steps.memory_tip: The two nearest adults: parents ease the pressure, teachers give the counselling.
steps.margin_note: Two named measures, one short block each.

steps.label: Peers and education
lines: Seek help from peers. If classmates see someone
falling into TDA abuse, they should bring it to
the notice of the parents or the teachers.
Education and counselling must be continuous.
Children should be taught about TDA at every
level in the form of regular lessons.
steps.why: Friends usually notice the change first, and steady teaching keeps the message going, so these two measures cover the gap the adults at home cannot see.
common_mistakes: Writing that friends should keep the matter secret. They should inform an adult.
Treating education as a single talk. The measure is continuous teaching.
steps.memory_tip: Friends report early, lessons keep repeating: both work before the habit forms.
steps.margin_note: Two more named measures. Keep each to two lines.

steps.label: Professional help
lines: Seek professional and medical help. Qualified
psychologists and psychiatrists, and de-
addiction and rehabilitation programmes, are
available.
With this help a person can come out of the
habit and return to a normal life.
steps.why: The last measure is the one used when prevention has already failed, and naming the trained people shows the student knows help exists beyond the family.
common_mistakes: Writing 'go to a doctor' with nobody named. Name the psychologist, the psychiatrist and the programmes.
Ending without saying the person can recover.
steps.memory_tip: When prevention fails, trained help follows: psychologist, psychiatrist, rehabilitation.
steps.margin_note: Name the three kinds of help in the box, then one closing line.

insider_note: Five named measures are printed in the book and the marks follow the count, so write them as separate named points rather than a paragraph.
